analysis.one_liner: Imposes a tiny 0.03% tax on each purchase of a stock, bond, or derivative to curb speculative trading and raise revenue.
analysis.headline: A 0.03% tax on stock, bond, and derivatives trades died in the Senate Finance Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have put a very small tax — 3 cents on every $1,000 — on each purchase of a stock, bond, or derivative in the U.S. or by a U.S. party. The idea was to slow down rapid-fire speculative trading and raise money from Wall Street transactions rather than from workers' paychecks. Companies raising money by issuing stock, and very short-term lending, would have been exempt. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the money would have come from banks, hedge funds, and high-frequency trading firms that execute huge numbers of transactions — a 0.03% tax is negligible for someone buying a house's worth of stock once, but adds up quickly for firms trading billions daily. The revenue raised could have reduced other taxes or funded public programs. Long-term investors would pay very little, since they trade infrequently.

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposed a 0.03% excise tax on purchases of stocks, bonds, and derivatives traded in the U.S. or involving a U.S. party, raising revenue from high-volume financial trading rather than from wages.
It covered derivatives — including options, futures, and contracts whose value is pegged to an index — so the tax would reach speculative instruments, not just plain stock purchases.
It exempted newly issued securities, very short-term debt (100 days or less), and certain securities lending, aiming the tax at secondary-market trading rather than at companies raising capital.

analysis.who_pays: Financial institutions and heavy traders — the tax is charged on every purchase of a stock, bond, or derivative, so the cost falls on the volume of trading. Some of it could be passed along to anyone who invests through funds, including retirement savers, though the rate is tiny per transaction.

drawbacks.text: The tax would raise trading costs for retirement savers indirectly: the tax is charged on every purchase of a stock, bond, or derivative, so fees on transactions by pension and mutual funds would rise slightly and could show up in small reductions in investment returns.

Because the tax applies only when the trade occurs in the U.S. or involves a U.S. party, some trading could move to foreign venues, and the bill directs regulators to write rules to prevent avoidance, which would be an ongoing enforcement challenge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — a tiny tax on high-volume trading that could raise tens of billions of dollars a year from the financial sector, mainly from high-frequency and speculative trading — was real, and the design (exemptions for initial stock issues and short-term debt, collection through exchanges and brokers) addressed some common objections. The drawbacks are real too: trading costs would rise somewhat for pension funds and mutual funds, and some trading would shift to untaxed foreign venues, shrinking both the revenue and any dampening of speculation. On balance the burden would have fallen mostly on the most active, most profitable corners of finance, not on ordinary savers.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced and immediately referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 2, 2011 and read twice before being referred to the Committee on Finance.
No further action was ever recorded; it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks, hedge funds, and high-frequency traders who would have paid the tax on every trade.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wall Street trading firms and hedge funds

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Iowa, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Wall Street Trading and Speculators Tax Act in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: All three supporters were progressive Democrats or an allied independent; no Republican cosponsor joined, and the Democratic-controlled Finance Committee never took the bill up.

industries.industry: Banks, hedge funds, and other high-volume securities traders
industries.note: The bill would have taxed each purchase of a stock, bond, or derivative at 0.03%, hitting high-frequency and speculative trading hardest. For a bill like this the tax is small per trade but large for firms executing millions of trades a day.

Derivative contracts and their payments would each count as taxable transactions, and exchanges and brokers would be responsible for collecting the tax. Derivatives speculation was squarely in the bill's crosshairs.
